title: Brazilian democratic satisfaction, institutional confidence, and partner preference move on different tracks before an election
source_unit: Pew Research Center survey of Brazilian adults, February 20-April 15, 2026

democratic_satisfaction.value: 37% satisfied and 59% not satisfied in spring 2026; satisfaction was 66% in 2013 and 16% in 2018
democratic_satisfaction.unit: percent of Brazilian adults across survey years

confidence_in_actors.value: 68% have not too much or no confidence in elected officials and 57% in business leaders; 73% express a lot or some confidence in professors and 70% in scientists
confidence_in_actors.unit: percent by institutional or social actor

partner_favorability.value: 47% favorable toward the U.S. and 46% favorable toward China in spring 2026; U.S. favorability fell from 64% in 2024 while China rose from 39% in 2023
partner_favorability.unit: percent favorable by country and year

ideological_partner_split.value: China favorable: 57% left versus 40% right; U.S. favorable: 30% left versus 58% right

observations.method: Nationally designed survey of Brazilian adults measuring democracy satisfaction, confidence in institutions and social actors, favorability toward China and the U.S., and ideological differences.
observations.uncertainty: The source is cross-sectional in 2026; comparisons across years may reflect political events, question context, or sample and field-period differences. Favorability toward trading partners does not establish trade behavior, policy alignment, or election choice.
observations.subgroup: Brazilian adults, with comparisons by ideological self-placement and support for the governing party coalition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low confidence in elected officials can coexist with stable democratic preferences, and equal favorability toward China and the U.S. can reflect diversification rather than geopolitical neutrality or realignment.

boundary: This record adds a pre-election public-meaning and partner-perception layer. It does not infer electoral outcomes, democratic performance, causal institutional decline, or foreign-policy alignment from opinion measures.
